title: Digital readiness for cardiovascular care in high-burden US communities with cardiology workforce constraints
desc: Digital health may extend cardiovascular care in communities with limited specialist access, but its effectiveness depends on whether communities have the infrastructure, devices, affordability, and capacity needed to use digital services. We linked national data on cardiometabolic disease burden, cardiology workforce, and digital readiness across 82,999 US census tracts. Among high-burden tracts in counties with no cardiologist or declining per-capita cardiologist supply, 4,765 (18.0%) tracts representing 19.9 million residents had higher digital readiness and were thus classified as deployment-priority tracts, whereas 21,752 (82.0%) tracts representing 74.1 million residents had lower readiness and were investment-priority tracts. Investment-priority tracts were spread across the urban-rural continuum and faced different barriers (adoption versus infrastructure). Contrasting classifications frequently occurred among neighboring census tracts within the same metropolitan area, highlighting geographic variation not captured by county-level targeting. Findings were broadly consistent across nine additional analyses with varying measures of readiness, workforce access, and classification thresholds. These findings provide a national framework for distinguishing communities where digital cardiovascular care may be deployed from those where infrastructure and adoption support may first be needed to enable equitable implementation. As presented at 2026 AHA Scientific Sessions: Analysis of U.S. Census and other national health data identifies communities with high cardiovascular care needs and assess health system readiness for digital care deployment.

title: Collaborative generalist-specialist AI for safe worklist deprioritization of non-contrast brain computed tomography
desc: Safe deprioritization of non-contrast brain computed tomography (NCCT) demands high sensitivity and negative predictive value (NPV) across common and uncommon findings requiring clinical attention. Here, we present a collaborative safety net integrating BrainCT-CLIP, a generalist foundation model via contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP), with commercial detectors. Every examination remained in the reporting workflow, deprioritized only when no model returned a positive result. In a retrospective multicenter external validation of consecutive emergency and trauma cohorts ( n = 2001), standalone commercial detectors left 31 of 324 remarkable examinations deprioritized, including 16 target-disease false negatives and 15 outside their indications. In contrast, the collaborative system recovered every remarkable examination at a threshold prespecified in the development cohort, achieving 100% sensitivity and NPV while deprioritizing 18% of examinations (368/2001; 95% CI, 17–20). These findings support generalist-specialist AI for safe worklist deprioritization under radiologist oversight, with high sensitivity for intracranial findings requiring clinical attention.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Gallbladder Carcinoma: A Review of Research Studies and Clinical Evidence.
desc: [Journal of gastrointestinal cancer] Gallbladder carcinoma (GBC) is the most common biliary tract malignancy and is usually diagnosed at an advanced stage. Artificial intelligence (AI), including radiomics, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), is increasingly applied to its diagnosis, surgical management and prognostication, but how far the reported performance can be trusted is unclear. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library and Google Scholar were searched to 5 May 2026 using database-specific search strategies. Each primary prediction-model study was characterized separately by design, number of centers and validation type (internal, temporal or external). Of 31 primary AI studies in GBC, 29 were retrospective, 22 were single-center and 24 reported internal validation only. In independent test or external cohorts, DL and ML models discriminated benign from malignant gallbladder lesions with areas under the curve (AUCs) of approximately 0.80-0.89; a multicenter model distinguishing xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis from GBC achieved an external AUC of 0.88, and automated computed tomography (CT) segmentation an external Dice score of 0.76. The best recurrence model achieved an AUC of 0.76 on internal (random-split) validation; none of the reviewed prognostic models reported a quantified external-validation estimate. Intraoperative AI is technically feasible but has no outcome data, and federated learning has been tested only in simulation. AI could plausibly assist several steps of GBC care, but the evidence is dominated by retrospective, single-center, internally validated studies from Asia, and metrics from different studies are not directly comparable. Prospective multicenter external validation, shared annotated datasets and standardized reporting are required before clinical adoption.

title: Application of Machine Learning and Deep Learning in diagnosis Covid19
desc: Predicting the progression of COVID-19 in hospitalised patients was an important challenge during the pandemic, particularly when healthcare resources were limited. This study investigates the use of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models to predict three clinical outcomes: death, admission to the intensive care unit (ICU), and clinical status (improvement or worsening). The study uses two patient datasets: an Algerian cohort of 80 patients from the Internal Medicine Department of the University Hospital Centre of Constantine, collected between July and August 2020, and a French cohort of 99 patients collected between March and May 2020. Five ML classifiers were evaluated: logistic regression (LR), k-nearest neighbours (KNN), classification and regression trees (CART), Naive Bayes (NB), and support vector machines (SVM). Their performance was examined in combination with three feature-selection methods: analysis of variance (ANOVA), mutual information (MI), and recursive feature elimination (RFE). The results were also compared with multilayer perceptron (MLP) models using one to five hidden layers. Model evaluation included 30 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation on the training data, followed by evaluation on a separate hold-out test set. The results showed that selecting 20 features generally provided better cross-validated accuracy than selecting 30 features or using the full feature set. The best-performing classifier-feature-selection combination varied across the six dataset-outcome tasks. LR combined with RFE was selected for three tasks, LR combined with ANOVA for one task, and CART combined with ANOVA for two tasks. The selected ML models achieved test-set accuracies ranging from 0.47 to 0.95 and higher accuracy than the average MLP results in five of the six tasks. These findings suggest that ML methods can be useful for exploring clinical outcomes in hospitalised COVID-19 patients. However, the small sample sizes and limitations of the available data mean that the results should be interpreted with caution. Further evaluation using larger and independent patient datasets is needed before these models can be considered for clinical use.

title: Leakage- and Label-Aware Benchmarking of Class-Imbalance Strategies for Multimodal Chest X-Ray and EHR Classification
desc: Benchmarks of class-imbalance strategies for multimodal chest X-ray (CXR) and electronic health record (EHR) prediction are often evaluated on record-level splits of cohorts in which one patient contributes several radiographs. We audit such a benchmark on 29,083 MIMIC-CXR radiographs of 10,479 patients with eight diagnosis targets. First, the record-split benchmark was misleading: a lookup table that copies the label of a development-set radiograph with the same EHR vector nearly matched the best model, and on unseen patients every model fell to the level of predicting every case positive. Second, tracing the labels back to MIMIC-IV explained why: each patient's labels are keyword matches on the diagnosis codes of a single admission, copied, with one EHR vector per patient, to all of the patient's radiographs, so about a third of the radiographs carry labels that differ from the codes of their own admission. Third, under patient-separated evaluation with admission-aligned and rule-refined labels, the initial conclusions do not hold: in the evaluated configurations no imbalance strategy raised the observed mean macro F2 over no augmentation by more than 0.01, tuned tree ensembles showed no consistent advantage over tuned logistic regression, and the released EHR variables stayed at the level of the all-positive baseline, whereas the diagnostic history available at imaging time and image embeddings exceeded it, including, with rule-refined labels, a CheXpert-trained encoder that never saw these radiographs; RAD-DINO had seen 96.6% of them during self-supervised pretraining. Adding either encoder to the diagnostic history gave no statistically significant F2 gain; exploratory AUROC gains were significant with RAD-DINO but not with DenseNet. We provide reusable diagnostics, a leakage-aware protocol and a checklist.

title: Multi-objective domain adaptation for pan-cancer transfer of pharmacogenomic drug response to patient tumours
desc: Large-scale pharmacogenomic screens provide rich drug-sensitivity measurements in cancer cell lines, but transferring these measurements to patient tumours remains limited by biological heterogeneity and cross-domain distribution shift. Existing machine learning approaches, including adversarial autoencoder and domain adaptation, address this gap by learning shared latent representations between preclinical models and patient samples. However, alignment without explicit biological constraints can produce unreliable representations when cancer lineage structure and clinically relevant patient heterogeneity are not preserved. Here, we introduce MODAE+, a pan-cancer multi-objective deep learning domain adaptation framework that jointly balances domain alignment, deconfounding, drug-response prediction, survival prediction, and cancer-lineage classification across 9,696 TCGA tumours, 1,293 CCLE cancer cell lines, and CTRP sensitivity profiles for 544 compounds in 738 matched cell lines. This multi-objective design improved cross-domain alignment while preserving cancer-lineage organization and patient heterogeneity. For drugs shared between the pharmacogenomic screen and TCGA treatment records, MODAE+ predicted sensitivity was significantly associated with overall survival among patients who received each drug in 46.3% of evaluated cancer-drug pairs by log-rank testing and 41.5% by multivariable Cox analysis. Biological validation across four curated drug-gene resources identified significant expression differences exceeding 1.5-fold for 34.9-64.4% of drugs in pan-cancer analyses, based on the lowest-p-value annotated gene per drug. Drug-class-specific patterns involved intended molecular targets for targeted therapies and predominantly transport, metabolism, detoxification and resistance-related genes for classical chemotherapies. As an additional validation, we derived pretreatment responder-nonresponder gene-expression signatures from 13 external breast cancer datasets and evaluated their concordance with MODAE+ predictions across 69 signature-drug comparisons in TCGA patients treated with paclitaxel or doxorubicin. Consensus signature scores showed Spearman correlations of 0.791 with predicted paclitaxel sensitivity and 0.724 with predicted doxorubicin sensitivity, averaging 0.758 across the two drugs. Opposing microbiome-mediated axes link modifiable lifestyles to health and chronic diseases
desc: Fecal shotgun metagenomics from 6,803 adults in the Japanese 4D cohort and microbiome-based prediction scores validated across 13 independent and geographically diverse cohorts revealed two opposing microbiome-mediated axes linking lifestyle to health and 15 diseases. Analyses disentangling the role of the gut microbiome in linking lifestyle factors to health outcomes remain limited. Here, using fecal shotgun metagenomics from 6,803 adults in the Japanese 4D cohort, we identified two opposing microbiome-mediated axes linking lifestyle to health and 15 diseases. A health-associated axis enriched in microbial metabolism of dietary components was linked to plant-based, soy and dairy intake. In contrast, a disease-associated axis, enriched in oral-derived bacteria and pathobionts, was linked to refined carbohydrates and sedentary behavior. Starter culture microorganisms used to ferment foods did not show statistically significant mediation of the observed health effects. Alcohol was associated with both health- and disease-oriented mediation patterns involving microbial host-glycan utilization. Microbiome-defined health- and disease-oriented mediator axes were supported by fecal short-chain fatty acids and plasma cytokines from >1,700 individuals, revealing butyrate-associated anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory host profiles, respectively. Microbiome-based prediction (MADE) scores captured lifestyle–microbiome–disease mediation patterns and distinguished individual diseases across 13 independent external cohorts from the United States, China, Sweden, Russia and Australia. We identify the gut microbiome as a key mediator linking lifestyle to health and disease, providing a framework for microbiome-based assessment to guide lifestyle interventions for health promotion and disease prevention.

title: AI-driven multi-horizon risk stratification for heart failure hospitalization in UA with HFpEF: a Chinese multi-center cohort study
desc: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) complicated by unstable angina (UA) represents a major challenge in chronic disease management with high risk of recurrent heart failure hospitalization (HFH), and despite the availability of multicenter real-world data, AI-driven tools for multi-horizon risk assessment remain limited. This multicenter retrospective cohort enrolled 4367 patients with UA and HFpEF, and an ensemble feature selection pipeline integrating LASSO, SVM-RFE and Boruta identified robust predictors, followed by training of twelve machine learning algorithms to estimate HFH risk at 12-, 24- and 36-month horizons with external validation. The optimal time-specific models (ET, GBDT and LightGBM) achieved strong discrimination in the training cohort with AUCs of 0.818, 0.834 and 0.863, and maintained performance in external validation with AUCs of 0.839, 0.836 and 0.851, respectively, while SHAP analysis highlighted diabetes mellitus, TyG-BMI and NT-proBNP as the most influential predictors. We developed and externally validated a multi-time-point machine learning framework for HFH risk stratification in UA and HFpEF, which showed acceptable calibration and potential clinical utility on decision-curve analysis. Further prospective and real-world validation across diverse populations and healthcare systems is needed to confirm clinical effectiveness and support translation into routine practice.

title: Applying artificial intelligence to optical coherence tomography for detection and subtyping of basal cell carcinoma.
source: PubMed · Journal der Deutschen Dermatologischen Gesellschaft = Journal of the German Society of Dermatology : JDDG
desc: [Journal der Deutschen Dermatologischen Gesellschaft = Journal of the German Society of Dermatology : JDDG] Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common cancer and a major public health burden. Noninvasive techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) may reduce unnecessary biopsies and enable earlier detection. However, effective OCT interpretation requires expertise. Artificial intelligence (AI) may help overcome this barrier. An AI model based on a U-Net convolutional neural network was trained using 4,680 annotated OCT image frames from 39 BCCs, 5,640 frames from 47 premalignant and benign lesions, and 12,360 frames from 103 scans of healthy skin. Detection performance was evaluated on an independent test set comprising 26 scans (3,120 frames) from 16 BCCs, 5 premalignant lesions, and 5 benign lesions. External validation used independent clinical data from 25 histologically confirmed BCCs (18 nodular, 7 superficial). AI-assisted OCT generated visual overlays corresponding to established BCC features and identified tumor areas. In the independent test set, the area under the ROC curve was 95.5 % for nodular and 98.2 % for superficial BCC. In clinical validation, all BCCs were detected, and subtype concordance with histology was achieved in 21 of 25 cases (83 %). AI-assisted OCT shows potential to improve non-invasive BCC diagnostics and warrants further clinical evaluation.

title: AI-Assisted Differentiation of Pancreatic Cystic Lesions Using EUS Images and Clinical Features
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Ruijin Hospital; conditions: Pancreatic Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm, Pancreatic Serous Cystic Neoplasm, Pancreatic Pseudocyst; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 400; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Pancreatic mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs), serous cystic neoplasms (SCNs), and pancreatic pseudocysts (PPCs) often exhibit overlapping imaging features on endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). However, these conditions require different clinical management strategies. Accurate differentiation is therefore important for appropriate treatment planning. This study aims to develop and validate an artificial intelligence (AI) model that integrates EUS images and clinical features to differentiate MCNs, SCNs, and PPCs. The study is designed as an ambispective observational diagnostic study consisting of retrospective model development, prospective temporal validation, and a reader study involving EUS physicians. Approximately 400 adult patients with confirmed MCN, SCN, or PPC will be included. Retrospective clinical data and EUS images will be used for model development and internal validation. After model development is completed, newly diagnosed patients will be prospectively enrolled to independently evaluate the diagnostic performance of the model. The primary outcome is the patient-level macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (macro-AUROC) for three-class classification in the prospective validation cohort. Secondary outcomes include diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, calibration, clinical net benefit, and the performance of EUS physicians with and without AI assistance. This study is expected to provide evidence for the potential clinical value of AI-assisted differentiation of pancreatic cystic lesions. No additional invasive procedures or study-specific treatments will be performed.

title: Figure format and the accuracy of AI-assisted reconstruction of Kaplan-Meier survival data
desc: Reconstructing participant-level data from published Kaplan-Meier curves supports meta-analysis and other secondary survival analyses when original trial records are unavailable. Researchers may use original PDF figures or screenshots, which can look alike but retain different information. We assessed how converting vector figures to images affects reconstruction by a language model that can inspect files and execute code. We generated 64 independent two-arm datasets across four scenarios combining 100 or 1,000 participants per arm with proportional or crossing hazards. Each figure was supplied as a native vector PDF and a matched 300-dpi PNG to Opus 5.5 through Claude Code under the same instructions. Outcomes compared reconstructed records with the original observed records: time-averaged absolute curve error through 24 months, error in the between-group restricted mean survival time difference, and error in the Cox log-hazard ratio. Native PDFs had lower curve error in all 64 completed pairs, including replacements for incomplete runs. Mean errors were 0.000029 and 0.1047 percentage points for PDF and PNG, respectively; the paired difference was -0.1047 (95% confidence interval, -0.1194 to -0.0909). PNG errors in the restricted mean survival time difference and log-hazard ratio were small: mean absolute errors were 0.0084 months and 0.0027. Lower resolution and compression increased curve errors; embedding unchanged pixels in a PDF did not restore vector accuracy. Some PNG runs exceeded the instructed revision limit, so results describe the implemented workflow rather than performance under a strictly enforced limit. Preserving vector information improved reconstruction fidelity in this workflow, but the observed differences do not establish clinically consequential changes in treatment estimates. Validation against reported survival summaries and event counts remains necessary. Generalization to published clinical figures and other model workflows requires further evaluation.

title: Enhanced MRI brain tumor detection using deep learning in conjunction with explainable AI SHAP based diverse and multi feature analysis
desc: Recent innovations in medical imaging have markedly improved brain tumor identification, surpassing conventional diagnostic approaches that suffer from low resolution, radiation exposure, and limited contrast. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is pivotal in precise and accurate tumor characterization owing to its high-resolution, non-invasive nature. This study investigates the synergy among multiple feature representation schemes such as local Binary Patterns (LBP), Gabor filters, Discrete Wavelet Transform, Fast Fourier Transform, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Gray-Level Run Length Matrix alongside five learning algorithms namely: k-nearest Neighbor, Random Forest, Support Vector Classifier (SVC), and probabilistic neural network (PNN), and CNN. Empirical findings indicate that LBP in conjunction with SVC and CNN obtained high specificity and accuracy, rendering it a promising method for MRI-based tumor diagnosis. Further to investigate the contribution of LBP, Statistical analysis chi-square and p-value tests are used to confirm the significant impact of LBP feature space for identification of brain Tumor. In addition, The SHAP analysis was used to identify the most important features in classification. In a small dataset, CNN obtained 97.8% accuracy while SVC yielded 98.06% accuracy. In subsequent analysis, a large benchmark dataset is also utilized to evaluate the performance of learning algorithms in order to investigate the generalization power of the proposed model. CNN achieves the highest accuracy of 98.9%, followed by SVC at 96.7%. These results highlight CNN's effectiveness in automated, high-precision tumor diagnosis. title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence rep-resentations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
desc: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly antibiotic resistance in bacterial pathogens, complicates infectious disease management. Because bacterial resistance is often mediated by protein functions, including antibiotic inactivation and efflux, protein sequence analysis provides a molecular basis for digital AMR surveillance and therapeutic intervention. We developed BacLLM, a language guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation-derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in WHO priority bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder. Compared with baselines, BacLLM provided more informative representations for resistance-gene identification and mechanism prediction, captured resistance associated mutational signals at single-residue resolution, and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC-centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending from AMR characterization to therapeutic prioritization, BacLLM also improved strain-level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a protein representation framework supporting AMR surveillance, functional characterization, and therapeutic candidate prioritization.

Exposure to legitimate and illegal online medicine vendors via search engines in 30 European countries
desc: Online medicine sales have not only improved access but also expose consumers to illegal online medicine vendors (IOMVs) selling substandard/falsified products. This study provides the first pan-European assessment of exposure to legitimate online pharmacies (LOPs) and IOMVs in search engine results (SERs). We scraped the top-50 Google results in 30 European countries for six tracer active pharmaceutical ingredients across three categories: controlled substances, prescription-only medicines (POMs), and over-the-counter products (OTCs). Links were categorised as LOPs or IOMVs based on official registries. From 9000 SERs, 3839 linked to medicine-selling websites (63.7% LOPs, 36.3% IOMVs). LOPs outnumbered and outranked IOMVs, though IOMV:LOP ratios reached 2.37 (Norway) and 2.18 (Cyprus). Search engine redirection affected 56.6% of IOMV links. IOMV prevalence increased with regulatory control: 1.4% (paracetamol), 5.5% (ibuprofen), 10.2% (omeprazole), 55.1% (amoxicillin), 76.2% (alprazolam) and 77.5% (clonazepam). IOMV links were less likely to be highest-ranked and less common in the top-10 SERs in countries permitting online OTC and POM sales, than in those prohibiting them. Despite LOP dominance, Europeans face substantial exposure to IOMV links, higher for controlled substances and in countries prohibiting online sales. Harmonised regulatory action, supported by search engine providers, is needed for safer online medication access.

title: Artificial intelligence in pediatric allergic diseases: what the clinician needs to know.
desc: [European journal of pediatrics] Artificial intelligence (AI) is reaching pediatric practice through consumer apps, wearables and decision-support tools, yet most children with allergic disease are managed by general pediatricians. This review summarizes what AI can and cannot do across pediatric allergic diseases, emphasising clinical readiness and the questions clinicians should ask before acting on an algorithmic output. Narrative review. MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus and Google Scholar were searched for English-language publications (January 2015-June 2026) on machine learning, deep learning, digital biomarkers and large language models in pediatric asthma, wheeze, atopic dermatitis, food allergy and allergic rhinitis. Peer-reviewed studies were appraised for clinical applicability, validation status and implementation barriers. Machine learning trajectory analyses show that allergic disease follows multiple coexisting pathways rather than a single atopic march. Deep learning interprets atopic dermatitis images and respiratory sounds with accuracy approaching specialist assessment. Predictive models estimate oral food challenge outcomes and impending asthma exacerbations, and wearable-derived biomarkers may signal deterioration early. Readiness nevertheless varies widely: most applications remain at research or pilot stage, constrained by small single-center datasets, scarce external validation, under-representation of darker skin tones, and limited interoperability with clinical workflows. AI is closer to the bedside in pediatric allergy than in many other areas of pediatrics, but few tools are ready for autonomous clinical use. No trial has yet shown that acting on an AI-derived risk estimate improves clinical outcomes in children. Pediatricians will increasingly encounter AI-derived outputs brought by families or embedded in health systems; appraising validation, representativeness and accountability is becoming a core clinical skill. • Pediatric allergic diseases follow heterogeneous trajectories that conventional tools predict poorly. • AI models report high accuracy in image, audio, and risk-prediction tasks. • Readiness, not reported accuracy, should govern clinical use: most tools remain research-stage. • Pediatricians need a practical framework to appraise AI outputs brought by families and health systems.

desc: Background. Middle and external ear disease is common and largely treatable, but accurate otoscopic interpretation requires training that is scarce outside specialist ENT services. Published deep learning models for otoscopy report high accuracy, yet most are optimised for closed set classification rather than the referral decision a non specialist actually makes, report uncalibrated probabilities, and do not report the near duplicate controls that video derived otoscopic datasets demand. We developed, validated and deployed a screening aid framed around referral rather than diagnosis. Methods. We merged 4,763 otoscopic images from 16 folders across three public datasets into 12 clinically meaningful classes. Every image was passed through a single field of view normalisation function (crop to the illuminated field, square, resize to 224 px, mask to one fixed circle) shared identically by training and inference, to remove the framing cue that otherwise identifies the source dataset. Because one source is video derived, images were grouped by cosine similarity of generic ImageNet features (threshold 0.93, joined transitively) and whole groups assigned to a single split, giving 3,326 training, 719 validation and 718 test images. A MobileNetV2 backbone initialised from ImageNet was fine tuned from block9expand. Probabilities were averaged over the eight dihedral transforms of each image and temperature scaled. The referral score was one minus the probability of a normal ear, and its threshold was set on the validation abnormal ears as the highest value still meeting a target sensitivity of 97%, applied with an inclusive comparison. Model selection, calibration and threshold were frozen before the test split was scored once. Results. On the 718 held out test images, referral sensitivity was 97.0% (95% CI 95.1 to 98.2) and specificity 75.6% (95% CI 69.4 to 80.8), with AUROC 0.974 for abnormal versus normal; a cluster bootstrap over the 363 similarity groups in the test split widens those intervals to 93.8 99.6% and 66.0 83.4% respectively. Of 501 abnormal ears, 15 were not referred; 11 of these were myringosclerosis and none was cholesteatoma. Twelve class macro F1 was 0.686, balanced accuracy 68.3%, and accuracy 85.0% (86.2% with chronic subtypes merged). Temperature scaling (T = 1.2) reduced expected calibration error from 0.0498 to 0.0430. A low confidence flag fired on 4.0% of test images, separating 87.2% accuracy on unflagged from 31.0% on flagged cases.

title: Scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification for Cancer Histopathology: Calibrated Uncertainty Under Distribution Shift
desc: Reliable uncertainty quantification is essential for clinical deployment of cancer diagnosis models, yet neural networks and variational Gaussian process methods can produce overconfident predictions, particularly under the distribution shifts that arise when models trained at one hospital are applied at another. We present a scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification (GPC) framework that operates on frozen pathology foundation model embeddings (Phikon) and combines accelerated Randomly Pivoted Cholesky (RPCholesky) for low-rank kernel factorization, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with non-centered parameterization for posterior sampling, and a pivots-as-inducing-points scheme for prediction. This makes HMC posterior sampling in the low-rank latent representation tractable at N approximately 300,000 training points, enabling HC-based low-rank GPC on substantially larger datasets than prior MCMC-based demonstrations. We evaluate on two histopathology benchmarks for breast cancer metastasis detection: PCam and CAMELYON17-WILDS, where the latter tests calibration under hospital-level distribution shift. Compared to stochastic variational GP and neural network baselines, our method improves calibration and predictive performance - reducing expected calibration error by up to 88% and false negative rate by up to 90% - with the largest gains appearing under distribution shift, suggesting that HMC-based posterior sampling provides more trustworthy uncertainty estimates for cross-site pathology classification.

title: Classifying tumors from broad category to hierarchical molecular subtype: an interpretable hierarchical framework for precision oncology
desc: Precise tumor subtype classification is important for guiding personalized treatment, characterizing tumor heterogeneity, and investigating molecular mechanisms. However, most existing multi-label classification models use flat architectures and do not fully exploit the inherent hierarchical relationships and biological constraints among tumor types, which limits their performance and interpretability in complex, fine-grained pan-cancer classification. Here, we present the cancer Hallmark-based Hierarchical Recursive Model (HHRM) for pan-cancer hierarchical multi-label classification. HHRM integrates hierarchical label structures with recursive neural networks, enabling simultaneous modeling of multi-level dependencies from broad cancer categories to specific subtypes. We trained the model on a comprehensive pan-cancer cohort of 11,476 samples spanning 26 primary cancer types and 405 subtypes across up to eight hierarchical levels. HHRM achieved an accuracy of 0.7924 for predicting hierarchical tumor subtypes and was further evaluated on a validation dataset of 887 samples. Compared with other hierarchical modeling frameworks, HHRM achieved higher accuracy in all three output modes. Ablation experiments showed that replacing the hallmark-based graph convolutional network reduced model performance. On an independent dataset of 1,608 breast cancer samples, HHRM also achieved an accuracy greater than 0.86. Finally, we combined SHAP with a network-based method to rank and analyze predictive genes at different levels of the tumor hierarchy, which identified both known and potentially novel biomarkers for cancer diagnosis. In conclusion, to our knowledge, HHRM is the first hierarchical model for multi-level tumor subtype classification. Its competitive performance, combined with post hoc biological interpretation, suggests potential value for precision cancer diagnosis.

External validation of an image-only ultrasound model for delivery-date prediction in four Chilean public hospitals
desc: Pregnancy dating fails the women who need it most: those who reach care without a first-trimester scan. We externally validated a commercial image-only ultrasound deep-learning model for delivery-date prediction, applied unmodified to 64,235 frames from 3788 examinations of 2550 pregnancies (34% migrant) at four Chilean public hospitals. Mean absolute error was 6.9 days versus 11.6 for the conventional due date, yet most of this gain reflected a shorter local gestation and fell below one day against recentred comparators. Fixed-term comparators assign every pregnancy the same gestational age at birth and therefore cannot rank who will deliver early, at any level of point accuracy: accuracy metrics are blind to the ranking on which management turns whenever the outcome distribution is concentrated, as in term-dominated cohorts. In a prespecified landmark analysis the model’s separate image-only risk score discriminated preterm birth with an area under the curve of 0.86, against 0.52 for gestational age alone; outside the landmark restriction it exceeded a clinical baseline of coded diagnoses plus same-examination biometry by 0.09, although it was miscalibrated. Error and calibration were also assessed by maternal nationality. These classification analyses are exploratory, and no woman was managed with the model; they identify what a prospective study should test.

title: A review of medical image segmentation research based on bibliometrics.
source: PubMed · Technology and health care : official journal of the European Society for Engineering and Medicine
desc: [Technology and health care : official journal of the European Society for Engineering and Medicine] BackgroundMedical image segmentation is a fundamental step in computer-aided diagnosis and treatment planning, and its research landscape has expanded rapidly with the advancement of artificial intelligence. A systematic bibliometric overview of this field is therefore needed to clarify its intellectual structure and emerging trends.ObjectiveTo provide a comprehensive bibliometric overview of the global research landscape, developmental trends, collaboration networks, and emerging hotspots in the field of medical image segmentation over the past decade.MethodsA bibliometric analysis was performed on 21,437 publications related to medical image segmentation, indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection from 2016 to 2025. The analysis systematically examined publication outputs, country-level contributions, author collaboration networks, journal distributions, and keyword co-occurrence patterns.ResultsThe annual publication count increased remarkably from 25 in 2016 to 5,207 in 2025. China contributed the largest share with 11,556 publications, followed by the United States (3,272) and India (1,924). Core researchers formed stable intra-team collaborations, though inter-team cooperation remained limited. Keyword and citation analyses identified deep learning, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), Transformers, U-Net, and their variants as dominant methodological themes. Case studies on skin and lung segmentation revealed differential research attention and international collaboration patterns across anatomical targets. A historical trajectory analysis showed methodological evolution from traditional image processing to fully convolutional networks and U-Net, and subsequently to hybrid architectures integrating attention mechanisms and Transformers.ConclusionMedical image segmentation has experienced substantial growth, driven by deep learning innovations. Future research may increasingly focus on multimodal foundation models capable of generalizable segmentation across diverse clinical scenarios. This bibliometric review offers researchers a valuable reference for understanding the intellectual structure and frontiers of the field.

desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: University of Southern California; conditions: Glaucoma; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 1386; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This randomized controlled trial will compare an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted teleglaucoma referral pathway with conventional referral among adults identified with referable glaucoma through the Los Angeles County Department of Health Services (LAC DHS) Teleretinal Screening Program. The primary objective is to determine whether AI-assisted referral reduces time to in-office diagnosis of manifest glaucoma. title: First-trimester nocturnal cardiorespiratory coupling during home sleep testing and later pregnancy complications: a secondary analysis of the nuMoM2b cohort
desc: We tested whether direction-specific nocturnal cardiorespiratory coupling (CRC) in the first trimester differed in pregnancies that later developed obstetric complications. The analysis included 2504 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort with valid level 3 home sleep recordings at 6-13 weeks' gestation. Bidirectional CRC between RR intervals and abdominal respiratory effort was quantified using bivariate phase-rectified signal averaging in consecutive 5-min segments. Coupling strength, local transition dynamics, and waveform irregularity were summarized by nightly mean and standard deviation. Associations with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM; n = 111), preeclampsia (n = 149), preterm birth (n = 192), and fetal macrosomia (n = 186) were examined using proportional-odds models with CRC feature quintile as the ordered outcome. Models included all four complications simultaneously and adjusted for maternal age, pre-pregnancy body mass index, race and ethnicity, gestational age at recording, relevant medical and family history, medication use, and apnea-hypopnea index >5 events/h. Holm correction was applied across outcomes. GDM was associated with lower respiration-to-heart rate coupling strength (cumulative odds ratio, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.31-0.64; P < 0.001) and shallower slope at the anchor point (0.63; 0.45-0.89; P = 0.03). Fetal macrosomia was associated with lower within-night variability in heart rate-to-respiration waveform irregularity (0.59; 0.45-0.77; P < 0.001). No associations with preeclampsia or preterm birth remained significant after correction. Direction-specific differences in nocturnal CRC were detectable in the first trimester in pregnancies that later developed GDM or resulted in fetal macrosomia.

title: Reclassification Is All You Missed: Surfacing Variant Reinterpretation Need in Online Health Communities at Population Scale
desc: Genetic variants are routinely reclassified in ClinVar after a patient is tested, sometimes from uncertain to pathogenic, yet patient recontact is inconsistent, with no clear duty and responsibility diffused among labs, providers, and patients. Many affected people discuss their results in public online health communities that clinical recontact often does not reach. We built PRISM, an agentic large-language-model pipeline that screens these posts, checks whether the variant was later reclassified, and drafts a disclaimer-bearing outreach message, in a no-contact dry run. Across 3.9 million posts from 32 communities, agent-predicted reinterpretation-relevant discussion is rare (0.288%) but concentrated in specialist genetics communities (6.30% versus 0.10% in general medical-advice communities) and growing fivefold since 2014; PRISM surfaces 123 candidate classification differences, 5 of them from an uncertain submission to pathogenic or likely pathogenic. On a held-out set of 30 real-post drafts, a clinician judged 27 factually grounded and 15 fit to send: factual accuracy is necessary but not sufficient for clinically acceptable outreach. PRISM contributes a population-scale reinterpretation-need map with code and data to be released upon publication.

title: Protify: A Benchmarking Platform Revealing Task Dependence and Homology Leakage in Protein Language Model Evaluation
desc: Protein Language Models (pLMs) have become essential tools for computational protein analysis, and the rapid proliferation of architectures, training objectives, and pretraining corpora has produced a diverse and expanding model landscape. Evaluation practices, however, remain fragmented: studies use different datasets, preprocessing pipelines, and reporting conventions, so results rarely transfer between publications. Here we introduce Protify, an open-source platform that standardizes pLM benchmarking across zero-shot, supervised, and transferlearning settings through a unified, low-code interface. Protify currently supports 35 pretrained models and 61 curated datasets and it is easy to add custom versions of each. Leveraging Protify's high throughput pipelines, we benchmarked 23 models on ProteinGym, discovering that DPLM3B is currently the top-performing self-supervised encoder. Another large-scale supervised evaluation across 32 diverse tasks, spanning enzyme classification, gene ontology annotation, protein-protein interaction, subcellular localization, and other functional properties, found that no single pLM dominated: 14 different models took the top score on at least one dataset, and the margins between the best and second-best models fell within run-to-run variability. On enzyme optimal pH prediction, a general-purpose probe pipeline matched or exceeded EpHod, a specialized model selected from 11,550 training runs, after 50 hyperparameter trials (R2 = 0.482 versus 0.425). Under a homology-controlled split of the same data, every pooled-embedding probe collapsed to near-zero R2, and only a transformer probe over full residue embeddings recovered appreciable signal (R2 = 0.248). Model rankings therefore depend as much on evaluation design as on the models themselves. Protify makes those design choices explicit, controlled, and replayable, and is freely available at https://github.com/Gleghorn-Lab/Protify.

Artificial Intelligence for Cardiovascular Health Behavior Change: A Narrative Review of Patient-Facing Tools.
source: PubMed · Health education & behavior : the official publication of the Society for Public Health Education
desc: [Health education & behavior : the official publication of the Society for Public Health Education] Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death in the United States and disproportionately affects racial/ethnic minoritized populations, low-income communities, older adults, and rural residents. Behavioral interventions can reduce cardiovascular risk, yet traditional programs face scalability barriers, including high costs and limited reach. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on the efficacy and equity of patient-directed AI tools that support health education and behavior change for cardiovascular health. Using PRISMA-ScR elements, we searched 10 databases (January 2010 to December 2025), yielding 19 empirical studies evaluating Generation 2.0 AI systems aligned with the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 (LE8) framework. Of these, five were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and 14 were nonrandomized (quasi-experimental, observational, or early-stage) studies. AI-enabled interventions such as conversational agents, machine-learning models, and reinforcement-learning systems addressed hypertension, diabetes, heart failure, and related conditions. Among the RCTs, one demonstrated superiority of an AI-powered program over usual care (AI-delivered Diabetes Prevention Program), whereas the remaining four reported outcomes equivalent or non-inferior to standard behavioral care. Effects were most apparent in high-intensity interventions that paired machine learning-based personalization with structured behavioral curricula, although the multi-component nature of these programs limits inference about AI-specific contributions. Across nonrandomized studies, greater engagement intensity was consistently associated with improved cardiometabolic outcomes, although causal attribution to AI-specific mechanisms remains limited. Most studies had small samples, short follow-up, and limited reporting on safety and equity. Technology-intensive interventions were concentrated in higher-resourced settings, and populations with limited health literacy showed reduced engagement. Overall, evidence supports cautious optimism that AI can meaningfully scale personalized cardiovascular prevention; however, realizing that equitable and clinically meaningful impact will require rigorous trials with longer follow-up, explicit behavioral science integration, safety-conscious governance, and equity-centered strategies addressing digital determinants of health.

title: Automated Vetting and Protocolling of MRI Examinations
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Edozie Iweka; conditions: Analysis of Retrospectively Collected MRI Referral Data; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 900000; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Background Vetting and assigning of protocols to MRI scan requests are usually carried out by radiologists and radiographers. This way is both time-consuming and prone to error. Recent improvements in Artificial Intelligence (Al) like Large Language Models (LLMs) are better at processing human language. It could be used to improve tasks like image reporting and assigning protocols in radiology. Approach Firstly, I will find out about the delays in the way this is currently done. I will use a survey to find out the perceptions of radiologists to both the current process and the proposed Al intervention. I will then use an LLM to undertake referral and protocol tasks. I will compare its performance to the performance of clinical specialists and established guidelines. I will present the explanation reports to radiologists and ask them if they can be understood and whether they can be trusted as clinically reliable. Impact My research could help reduce the workload and time radiologists spend dealing with scan requests. The findings will help design future research to consider application in real clinical settings.

title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model
desc: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $θ$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.

title: A protein language model for domain, functional site, and variant effect prediction
desc: Protein sequence databases are growing far faster than experimentally curated annotations, limiting functional interpretation of newly identified proteins and coding variants. We developed PALM, a protein annotation language model that jointly predicts domain and functional-site occurrence, while preserving overlapping and nested annotations through a soft-target objective. PALM integrates ESM2 with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), learned layer aggregation, and a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) encoder. PALM was trained on ~15 million InterPro-annotated UniRef50 sequences spanning 17,951 domain and 1,383 site classes. Across 2.3 million held-out proteins, PALM achieved domain- and site-occurrence F1 scores of 0.941 and 0.877, respectively, and retained substantial performance in proteins with <20% sequence identity to the training and validation data. PALM also substantially outperformed ESM3 annotation baseline. Without training on variant-pathogenicity labels, PALM embedding disruption distinguished 151,823 ClinVar missense variants more accurately than ESM2 embedding disruption (AUROC 0.835 versus 0.710), and combining PALM embedding disruption with the ESM2 likelihood-ratio signal reached an AUROC of 0.877. The same combined zero-shot score outperformed AlphaMissense on a benchmark dataset on 128,161 missense variants, that were derived from literature but not present in ClinVar database. At the protein level, PALM embeddings showed stronger CATH-Gene3D superfamily organization than frozen ESM2 and ESM3 embeddings, and improved prediction of experimental activation and repression effects when combined with ESM2. In a downstream case study, we demonstrated the ability to use PALM-derived embedding as proxy of deep mutational scanning (DMS), showcasing the broad application of PALM. Together, PALM converts curated residue-level knowledge into transferable and mechanistically interpretable representations that connect protein sequence, function, and variant consequence.

Green AI for Telehealth.
desc: [Healthcare management forum] Telehealth is increasingly supported by connected devices, remote monitoring, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and distributed computing. These tools can extend access and support more responsive care, but their computational and environmental demands are rarely considered alongside clinical and organizational needs. We describe the current Canadian telehealth landscape, including remote care management, virtual visits, patient portals, and remote monitoring, and identify opportunities and gaps for AI integration. We then define Green AI in healthcare and explain how an IoT-fog-cloud architecture can support resource-aware telehealth. For health leaders, Green AI is not only an engineering issue. It affects procurement, infrastructure planning, workforce capacity, clinical workflow, environmental responsibility, and equity. Evaluation should consider clinical performance, resource use, organizational fit, and sustainability. Responsible AI-enabled telehealth requires more than technical performance. A Green AI perspective can help health organizations improve computational efficiency while maintaining patient safety, usable workflows, resilience, and equitable access.

title: Accuracy and Time Efficiency of AI Versus Manual Segmentation in Adult Crowding Using Aligner Software
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Dina ahmed; conditions: Dental Crowding; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 155; status: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] The purpose of this study is to evaluate how accurately and quickly artificial intelligence (AI) can separate individual teeth from digital dental scans of adults with dental crowding. The study will compare AI-based tooth segmentation with manual segmentation performed by experienced orthodontists. Digital dental scans from adult patients with moderate to severe dental crowding will be analyzed. The scans will be processed using two orthodontic software programs, Archform 2.6.4.1 and Blue Sky Plan V5, which use AI to automatically identify and separate individual teeth. The same scans will also be manually segmented by experienced orthodontists. The study will compare the results from the different methods by assessing whether the teeth are correctly identified and separated, the accuracy of tooth measurements, the types of segmentation errors, and the time required to complete the segmentation. The study aims to determine whether AI-based segmentation can provide accurate results while reducing the time required for digital orthodontic analysis. The findings may help improve the efficiency of digital orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning, particularly for adults with crowded teeth.

title: What Patients Say They Can't Access: Mining Cancer Screening Barriers from Online Communities
desc: Cancer screening disparities persist across the U.S., yet the patient-reported barriers driving low uptake remain poorly characterized at scale. While clinical surveys capture structured responses, they miss the organic, unsolicited discourse where patients candidly describe real-world obstacles. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale analysis of over 56,000 posts across six cancer-specific Reddit communities to surface barriers to cancer screening among U.S. patients. We apply a pipeline combining keyword filtering, barrier triage, open coding, and codebook synthesis to systematically extract and categorize patient-reported barriers from 576 U.S.-located posts. Our qualitative analysis reveals recurring structural, informational, and psychosocial barriers that vary meaningfully by cancer type and community context. These findings lay the groundwork for future work aimed at proactively identifying and addressing barriers at scale - spanning a broader range of cancer types and populations - and informing the design of targeted interventions, navigator programs, and health system policies that translate patient-reported obstacles into actionable solutions.

title: FeatureMAP enables network-guided interpretation of untargeted metabolomics
desc: Untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) metabolomics generates thousands of features, but incomplete metabolite annotation and reliance on predefined pathways limit their biological interpretation. Here we present FeatureMAP, an LC-MS feature-centric computational framework that integrates multi-evidence metabolite annotation, network-guided refinement, metabolic module discovery, and structured large language model-based functional interpretation. Across ten public datasets, FeatureMAP improved MS1-based metabolite candidate prioritization while reducing annotation redundancy. In semi-synthetic benchmarks, FeatureMAP recovered coordinated metabolic perturbations, achieving 92% recovery of a simulated perturbation, and distinguished concurrent metabolic processes. Controlled benchmarks further evaluated functional interpretation under competing metabolite-level signals. Based on FeatureMAP, we additionally developed PhenoMAP, a phenotype-aware knowledge graph comprising 12,929 dysregulated metabolic modules from 501 human metabolomics studies spanning 326 phenotypes. Module-level comparisons revealed reproducible metabolic similarities across independent studies and biologically supported relationships among phenotypes. Application to Alzheimer's disease cerebrospinal fluid and cellular datasets identified convergent membrane-lipid alterations and implicated galactose-linked glycosphingolipid remodeling. Together, FeatureMAP and PhenoMAP enable network-grounded interpretation of incompletely annotated LC-MS metabolomics data and systematic investigation of metabolic dysregulation across biological conditions.
